Question: Why don't we observe Planck's constant in our day-to-day experiences?
Answer: We don’t observe Plank’s constant (h) for the same reason we don’t observe all the other physical constants (we don’t observe Coulomb’s constant either, for instance) or the physical quantities (we don’t “observe” energy!). We observe the physical phenomena and then we measure or calculate the quantities and constants related to them. The physical constants are quantities related to phenomena, have physical value and units (Plank’s constant is related to the energy of photons), can be measured experimentally or calculated theoretically, and have the same value in all frames of reference, unlike the “usual” physical quantities. Question: How can you pursue freedom for yourself while providing value for others?
Answer: And freedom is??? I’ve always wondered what the Anglo-Saxons mean by this term; in Greek, the meaning is clearer, freedom is what is to come but isn’t here yet; let’s say that freedom resembles a lot of hope or release. So, I’ll answer the Greek way. When we try to uplift other people, we do it because we love them and choose to do so freely. We see it as a kind of battle against misery of all kinds because we need to give hope/freedom to others. Freedom is not an individual good; it is communal. For you to become free of your mental bounds, I must be also free so that I help you break them. If we succeed, I’ll be a better person too. It’s freedom for both or none; togetherness.

Question: What process took city states from monarchy to aristocracy and in Athens to democracy?
Answer: There is not an easy or definite answer to this question as we lack evidence for crucial periods and events. At least, I’ll try to make my answer short, following the evolution of the Greek regimes step by step beginning from the Bronze Age and the proto-Greeks, the Mycenaeans. Step 1: The Mycenaean monarchy was not a strict monarchy; true, there was a king (the wanax) but the damos (the people’s assembly) is referred to in the Linear B tablets as having some limited power (eg., the land belonged to the state and the wanax couldn’t use it unless the damos’ decided on it). It is clear that even in the Bronze Age, the citizens participated (or at least, were present) in the decision-making of the state. Around 1100 BCE, this regime vanished. Evidence of riots is found, the wanax perished, and many members of the nobility fled away. Vouleutirion (assembly place, “parliament”) from pre-historic Poliochni, Lemnos. Image from Photos of Poliochni Lemnos Step 2: The dim Geometric period; still one leader, a king (c.1100-700 BCE) And now what, after the distraction of the Mycenaeans? Truth be told, we don’t know much. In this early Greek period, the lack of writing cost us a lot. The archaeological findings show the formation of the city-states as we know them. They are governed by one leader, most probably, the successors of the Mycenaean local governors, the vasileus, a king. We can only assume, judging from the Homeric epics, writings by later ancient authors, and tradition that the institution of the damos (demos from now on) kept on and the noble families (remnants of the Mycenaean years) formed a consulting group, the gerousia. Step 3: Aristocracy, the nobles get the power From this time point, each city-state took a different path; some, like Sparta and Macedonia, kept the kingship whereas others, the majority, proceeded with more reforms. In most cities the power of the king is limited gradually, leading to its abolition, mainly restricted by the desire of other members of noble and wealthy families to have a share in power. In Corinth, eg., it became an annual kingship first, limited to members of this lineage. That is, instead of the king holding his office for life, there is a rotation of members of this specific family in the position of the king. In the case of Athens, c. 752/1 BCE, the lifelong kingship abolished and is replaced by rulers with a ten-year term, who, however, came from the royal lineage. The ten-year rule of the king becomes an annual magistracy (682 BCE), and gradually, nine offices are created. One of them is the Archon Basileus, a remnant of royal office, even only by name. Aristocracy (=the power to the nobles) had emerged. More institutions of authority are established, such as the voule (parliament) and the Areopagus. All members are still aristocrats but have to be elected. In this period, one more revolutionary event happened; the Greeks started to write again. Among the first texts were the laws of each city. Written on public walls, they were accessible to every citizen. Although the first laws concerned mostly family, inheritance, and economic rights, they indirectly affected the political system, as they determined when a resident of the city was simultaneously a citizen (differences exist from city to city). In addition, being written in public and known to all somewhat limited the predatory disposition of the nobles. The law of Dreros is the earliest recorded European law (650–600 BCE). Image credit the Constitutional Law of Dreros: The Earliest Surviving Greek Law on Stone Although ten aristocrats (instead of one) were in charge and happy about it, the middle class and, mainly, the farmers were furious with the administration; the financially struggling among them lost their farms and even their freedom due to debts. As if that weren't enough, complaints about injustices against the weak were numerous (the references to by Hesiod are characteristic). Step 4: Democracy Some city-states attempted to alleviate the explosive situation through colonies. Others, like Athens, proceeded with reforms mainly focusing on the economic and legal framework of each class. However, inevitably, political rights were granted to the middle and lower class for the first time (~600 BCE). A note: That wasn’t out of courtesy; in ancient Greece, citizenship was tightly related to the ability to be under arms. As the Athenian soldiers paid for their armor themselves, whoever participated in the army (the middle class) demanded more political rights. Gradually, as more and more Athenians joined the army, all were granted full rights c.460 BCE, meaning that all the Athenians could be elected and vote, no matter their financial status or their family’s origin. The recent Persian Wars and the oncoming clash with Sparta convinced everyone that the military power, and therefore the entirety of the Athenian citizens, had to be as strong as possible. EDIT: Democracy was not a miracle, as it didn’t happen suddenly nor is inexplicable. However, an attempt to follow all the events one by one in detail (and explain their cause) would make this answer extremely long and I may say extremely boring. So, I chose to write a very brief summary, avoiding dates and names…

Question: Does everyone need a bit of cynicism in their character?
Answer: Oh yes! Yes, yes, yes. Do I sound cynical? Cynicism today is about casting doubts on other peoples’ motives. An example: I may say that I gave a sizable donation to rebuilding Notre Dame because I care about its enduring religious, historical, and cultural significance in and beyond France. The cynic, says that I did so because it made me look good, distracted public attention from my unsavory business practices perhaps and it helped my tax return. The cynic examines the other (“darker” and not published) side of my donation, devalues the moral currency, chipping away at or adulterating the metal base and he can be right. In layman’s terms, a cynic is a thinker who doesn’t “swallow” at once everything they’re served. This is a good thing, can be very constructive but don’t overdo it, doing it too often is likely to get us into trouble. So, yes but, as you said, a bit. Old And Cynical Cartoons and Comics

Question: Where does the Athenian Parthenon Temple get its name?
Answer: We don’t know! But, there are some theories about it; a. Parthenon may mean ‘the temple of the virgin goddess’ as Athena was one of the virgin (another term with unclear meaning) goddesses. There is an issue in this one as the adjective virgin was mainly used for Artemis, not Athena, who was named Polias or Pallas. b. It was named after a room located in the west cella of the temple. Some scholars argue that it was the place where the sacred veil was worn on the statue of Athena by the Arrephores, a group of four virgin girls chosen to serve their city each year during the Panathenaia. Do you see the small room in the back of the temple? That was the girls’ room. Other scholars claim that they resided in the Erechtheion. Image from Πώς σώθηκε ο Παρθενώνας το 1821 c. The term may be a reference to the virgin daughters of King Cecrops who sacrificed their lives to save the city. We don’t know when the temple was named Parthenon either. The architects Iktinos and Kallikratis (5th century) seem to have referred to the building as "Hekatompedos" (Cathedral) in their lost treatise on Athenian architecture, and during the 4th century onwards, the building was referred to as "Hekatompedos" or "Hekatompedon" as well as "Parthenon". The first source in which the temple is characterized as the Parthenon is a text by the orator Demosthenes in the 4th century BCE. Plutarch (1st century CE) referred to the temple as "Hekatompedos Parthenon". Note: The notion that the Parthenon was named as such during the Christian period is wrong, the Christian temple was dedicated to Panaghia Atheniotissa (Holy Mary of Athens).
